whoa.headline: A day on Venus is longer than its year
whoa.summary: Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes longer than one trip around the Sun. Sunrise there is a rare event.
whoa.try: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.
whoa.tryLine: Earth: 24 hours. Venus: about 243 Earth days. Say that out loud.

whoa.headline: A straw works because of air, not magic suck
whoa.summary: You lower the pressure in your mouth. Outside air pushes the drink up the straw. Space has no air push, so straws fail there.
whoa.try: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.
whoa.tryLine: Pinch the top of a full straw. The drink stays. That's air pressure.

whoa.headline: She spotted a supernova at 14
whoa.summary: Caroline Moore was 14 when she found an exploding star in another galaxy. She used a backyard-style telescope network and careful checking. Pro astronomers confirmed it.
whoa.try: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.
whoa.tryLine: Look up 'supernova' images. That's a star's last big shout.

whoa.headline: Fold a T-shirt in two seconds
whoa.summary: Pinch the shoulder and the mid-chest, flip it over the other shoulder, then fold. Once you have the pinch points, it looks like a trick.
whoa.try: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.
whoa.tryLine: Race a messy pile. Time the first three shirts.

whoa.headline: You interrupted and the room went quiet
whoa.summary: Own it fast: 'Sorry - finish your bit.' Then wait. That one line turns an oops into respect.
whoa.try: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.
whoa.tryLine: Practise it once so it is ready when you need it.

whoa.headline: Penguins propose with a pebble
whoa.summary: Some penguins hunt for a smooth pebble and drop it at a partner's feet. If the pebble is accepted, that is a yes. Romance, but rocky.
whoa.try: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.
whoa.tryLine: If you see penguins in a film, watch for the pebble handover.

whoa.headline: Your body makes a new skeleton every 10 years
whoa.summary: Bone is not a dead stick. Cells nibble old bone and lay new bone. The skeleton you have at 20 is not the same material you had at 10.
whoa.try: Jump. That's the system answering back.
whoa.tryLine: Jump. That's the system answering back.

whoa.headline: Learn one useful knot: the bowline
whoa.summary: The bowline makes a loop that does not slip. Boats, trees, and rescue lines use it. Rabbit out the hole, around the tree, back down.
whoa.try: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.
whoa.tryLine: YouTube 'bowline' with a shoelace. Make three in a row.

whoa.headline: He built a Braille printer from Lego
whoa.summary: Shubham Banerjee was 13 when he made a cheap Braille printer using Lego Mindstorms so more kids could afford books they can feel.
whoa.try: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?
whoa.tryLine: Close your eyes and read a cereal box by shape. Hard, right?

whoa.headline: Velcro is a burr that said yes
whoa.summary: A Swiss engineer pulled burrs off his dog and looked under a microscope. Tiny hooks. He copied them. Your trainers are wearing a plant idea.
whoa.try: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.
whoa.tryLine: Find a burr on a walk. That's the original Velcro.

whoa.headline: Someone is left out at lunch
whoa.summary: You do not need a speech. 'Want to sit with us?' is enough. If they say no, you still planted a door.
whoa.try: Use it once this week. One sentence.
whoa.tryLine: Use it once this week. One sentence.

whoa.headline: A teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh a mountain
whoa.summary: The leftover core of a giant star is packed past imagining. A spoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes. Gravity won that argument.
whoa.try: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a teaspoon. Now imagine it weighing more than everyone you know.

whoa.headline: An octopus has three hearts
whoa.summary: Two hearts pump blood to the gills. The third pumps blood to the rest of the body - and it actually stops when the octopus swims.
whoa.try: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?
whoa.tryLine: Ask someone: why would a heart stop on purpose?

whoa.headline: Planes don't float. They steal lift from air.
whoa.summary: The wing is curved so air on top moves faster and pushes less. Air underneath pushes more, and that extra push is lift. Same idea as holding your hand out a car window.
whoa.try: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.
whoa.tryLine: Next car ride, tilt your hand like a wing and feel it climb.

whoa.headline: A 14-year-old built a windmill from scrap
whoa.summary: William Kamkwamba's village in Malawi had almost no electricity. He used a library book, a broken bicycle, and junkyard parts. The windmill lit his house and pumped water.
whoa.try: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?
whoa.tryLine: What broken thing in your house could still do a job?

whoa.headline: Tell if an egg is still good in 5 seconds
whoa.summary: Drop it in a glass of water. Fresh eggs sink and lie on their side. Old eggs stand up. Bad eggs float - throw those away.
whoa.try: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.
whoa.tryLine: Test one egg from the fridge tonight.

whoa.headline: Your friend got the part you wanted
whoa.summary: First feeling: unfair. Good move: "Congrats. You earned it." Then ask the teacher what to practise for next time. You look strong, and you get a plan.
whoa.try: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.
whoa.tryLine: Practise that one line out loud. It feels weird. That's normal.

whoa.headline: You cannot tickle yourself. Your brain blocks you.
whoa.summary: Your brain predicts your own fingers, so the surprise is gone. Tickling needs a tiny "I didn't see that coming." That's why another person works and you don't.
whoa.try: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.
whoa.tryLine: Try it anyway. Then try to tickle a parent who isn't ready.

whoa.headline: A lightning bolt is hotter than the surface of the sun
whoa.summary: The sun's surface is about 5,500°C. A lightning bolt can hit 30,000°C. That's why it turns air into a flash and a boom you hear later.
whoa.try: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.
whoa.tryLine: Next storm, count the seconds after the flash. Divide by 3 for kilometres.

whoa.headline: She built a flashlight that runs on body heat
whoa.summary: Ann Makosinski was 15. She made a hollow flashlight with no batteries - just the heat from your hand. It won a big science fair and actually worked.
whoa.try: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.
whoa.tryLine: Hold a metal spoon. Notice it feels colder than wood. That's heat leaving your hand.

whoa.headline: A lock is just a bunch of tiny lifts
whoa.summary: Your key is a row of hills. Each hill lifts a pin to the exact right height so the cylinder can turn. Wrong key = one pin still blocking.
whoa.try: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.
whoa.tryLine: Look at a house key. Those jagged bits are the hills.

whoa.headline: The 60-second room reset
whoa.summary: Set a timer. Clothes on the chair, rubbish in the bin, stuff you used back where it lives. Don't clean. Just reset. Most rooms look 80% better in one minute.
whoa.try: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.
whoa.tryLine: Do it once tonight. See if it feels like a magic trick.

whoa.headline: Someone laughs at your idea
whoa.summary: Don't laugh at yourself to join in. Try: "Okay, but I'm still going to try it." Short. Calm. You didn't attack them, and you didn't drop the idea.
whoa.try: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on something small this week, even a game idea.

whoa.headline: Your brain dumps the mission mid-walk
whoa.summary: You stand up, walk into a room, and forget why. Doorways actually reset a bit of your memory. Your brain files "kitchen plan" and starts "hallway plan."
whoa.try: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.
whoa.tryLine: Say the mission out loud before you walk. "Glass of water." It sticks better.

whoa.headline: "Look up at the stars and not down at your feet."
whoa.summary: Stephen Hawking said that. He meant: spend your brain on big, interesting things, not on small worries. You can do both in one night - homework, then 2 minutes of sky.
whoa.try: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.
whoa.tryLine: Tonight, step outside and find one thing in the sky you can name.

whoa.headline: Tardigrades can survive outer space
whoa.summary: These tiny "water bears" can dry out, freeze, and even go into space with no suit - then wake up later and walk around. They are almost impossible to kill.
whoa.try: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.
whoa.tryLine: Look up a tardigrade photo. It looks like a chubby eight-legged bear.

whoa.headline: At 13 he built a radio station from junk
whoa.summary: Kelvin Doe lived in Sierra Leone with almost no money for parts. He made batteries from acid, soda and metal, then a transmitter from scrap. Neighbours tuned in to his station for music and local news. MIT later invited him to show how he did it.
whoa.try: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?
whoa.tryLine: Pick one broken gadget at home. Can you name 3 parts inside it?

whoa.headline: The game already started without you
whoa.summary: Don't hover. Walk up and say "Got room for one more?" If they say not this round: "Cool, I'll jump in next." Then watch like a teammate, not like a sad statue.
whoa.try: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.
whoa.tryLine: Use it at break. The sentence is the whole trick.

whoa.headline: Wi - Fi is just shouted numbers, very fast
whoa.summary: Your router yells invisible radio blips. Your phone listens and turns the blips back into pictures and words. Walls eat some of the yell, which is why the signal dies in the bathroom.
whoa.try: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.
whoa.tryLine: Stand next to the router, then behind a wall. Watch the bars change.

whoa.headline: Cows pick a best friend - and stay calmer together
whoa.summary: Scientists found many cows choose one favourite cow and hang out with them. Smart farms keep those pairs together, because friend-cows eat better and stay healthier. Even cows know a good teammate helps.
whoa.try: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.
whoa.tryLine: Next time you see cows, watch who stands next to who.

whoa.headline: Remember any name with one trick
whoa.summary: When you meet someone, say their name back once: "Cool, I'm ___, hi Maya." Then stick it to a picture in your head - Maya with a map. People light up when you get it right next time.
whoa.try: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.
whoa.tryLine: Use it on one new person this week. Just the repeat is enough.

whoa.headline: There are more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy
whoa.summary: The Milky Way has around 100 billion stars. Earth has about 3 trillion trees. We still cut them down too fast - but the planet is greener and stranger than it looks from a car.
whoa.try: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.
whoa.tryLine: Guess how many trees you can see from your window. Then count.

whoa.headline: Hunt: one free kids thing this week
whoa.summary: Libraries, museums and parks quietly run free drop-ins. Pick one, show up, stay 20 minutes. That counts as an adventure.
whoa.try: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.
whoa.tryLine: Ask a parent to search free kids events this weekend plus your town.

whoa.headline: RoboCup 2026: Why are robots playing football in Germany?
whoa.summary: RoboCup 2026 took place in Germany this year. BBC reporter Andrew Rogers was there and asked a robotics expert all about it.

whoa.headline: Happy News: Stories to make you smile
whoa.summary: De-Graft has this week's Happy News. We are visiting an autumnal festival in Vietnam, a community garden in Australia and meeting some showbiz pumpkins in Germany.

whoa.headline: Venus ate its moon: How Earth's 'twin' could have swallowed a rocky satellite
whoa.summary: Scientists have long speculated why Venus, with a size, mass and structure similar to Earth's, doesn't have a moon. New UC Riverside research shows that our hungry twin likely swallowed it.

whoa.headline: To understand the solar cycle, notice how the sun sleeps
whoa.summary: The sun is such a constant in our lives that it can be difficult to imagine our star ever changing. But the sun can be quite variable. There are times when its magnetic field is turbulent and generates many sunspots and other times when it is quiet and dormant.

whoa.headline: Strictly is back - were you watching?
whoa.summary: Fifteen celebrities have joined for the 24th series, but this year there have been some changes with celebs partnered with their professionals dancers in a new way and there have also been changes to the presenting line-up. Let us know what you thought of this year's launch show.

whoa.headline: Scientists simulate cosmic crashes to test whether icy moons gain or lose their ability to sustain life
whoa.summary: Many of the moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus and Neptune likely conceal oceans of liquid water beneath miles of icy shell. Because life as we know it needs water, these buried oceans rank among the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth.

whoa.headline: Will Youth Parliament be forced to close?
whoa.summary: The UK Youth Parliament is made up of a group of 300 elected young people aged between 11 and 18. Their job is to speak up about issues that matter to young people in their area, hold debates, make speeches and run campaigns about all kinds of topics, from schools to health and the environment. Find out why the parliament may need to close, here.

whoa.headline: Are you taking part in the Great British Beach Clean?
whoa.summary: An environmental charity is asking people to pick up their gloves and bin bags and head to the beach.

whoa.headline: Hubble spots an out-of-sync galaxy
whoa.summary: Though the spiral galaxy in this new image from the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It's one of more than a thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.

whoa.headline: COSI Telescope Comes Together
whoa.summary: UC Berkeley engineers and managers watch as the COSI (Compton Spectrometer and Imager) detector assembly is slowly raised from a table in this July 8, 2026, image.

whoa.headline: From the start, the solar system chose fire over ice to build its first bodies
whoa.summary: When the solar system first took up the task of building solid bodies - such as planets, moons and protoplanets - it basically had a choice between two ingredients: heat-forged chondrules, which were millimeter-sized bits of rock, and matrix, a fine-grained, cold dust loaded with water ice and organic molecules. And from the get-go, the solar system chose fire.

whoa.headline: First new wild cat species discovered in more than 100 years
whoa.summary: Experts say 'Leopardus tilcayo' is around the size of a domestic cat, but its spotted and striped coat initially made it difficult to tell it apart from other wild cats in the area. Find out more here.

whoa.headline: Five Ways the World of the Dinosaurs Looked Different From Ours, Beyond the Presence of the 'Terrible Lizards'
whoa.summary: Earth has changed dramatically since the Age of Dinosaurs, from its climate to geography and animal life

whoa.headline: The human brain may owe a lot of its size to our love of sweets
whoa.summary: Our sweets cravings may have set the stage for the human brain to become big and powerful. That's the finding of a new study. The brains of our upright-walking ancestors, some 4 million years ago, weighed only around 300 grams (11 ounces).

whoa.headline: Why is the UK so bad at Eurovision? Politicians want answers
whoa.summary: The UK has struggled at Eurovision for years. Now MPs want to know if song choices, performances or the way acts are selected are to blame.

whoa.headline: A galaxy spinning out of sync
whoa.summary: Image: Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It's one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.

whoa.headline: De-Graft gets a special visit from Gardeners' World
whoa.summary: See what happened when a team of gardening experts visited De-Graft's allotment plot to give it some much needed attention.

whoa.headline: Strange News: The weirdest stories of the week
whoa.summary: Shanequa has this week's feast of Strange News. We've got the toughest rowing race you'll ever see, some clowning around in Brazil, and robots strutting their stuff on the catwalk.

whoa.headline: New krypton-88 data narrow a key gap in stellar strontium models
whoa.summary: An international research team has reported the first experimental investigation of a nuclear physics reaction essential for understanding how the element strontium is produced in stars - specifically in stellar environments where traditional explanations for its formation fall short. The study, published June 8 in Communications Physics, reports that the team used indirect experimental techniques to extract previously inaccessible information about how an isotope of a separate element - krypton - absorbs, or captures, neutrons.

whoa.headline: A glimpse of the solar system's origins: Striking details on the molecules inside a meteorite
whoa.summary: Researchers at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory and Brookhaven National Laboratory have teamed up to get a fresh look at the complex makeup of meteorites and glimpse into our solar system's past.

whoa.headline: NASA Unveils Enterprise, the First Space Shuttle
whoa.summary: The rollout ceremony for NASA's first space shuttle, OV-101, coincided with Constitution Day of the nation's bicentennial on Sept.17, 1976. Although the orbiter was originally planned to be named Constitution, Star Trek fans successfully convinced President Gerald Ford to name it Enterprise after the series' fictional starship.

whoa.headline: A modern 'snowball' Earth? What the movies get wrong
whoa.summary: Earth has frozen over in the past - at least five times. Science fiction is full of takes about how it might happen again and the implications of a modern ice age. The problem: At a minimum, sci-fi gets the timetable for Earth turning into a "snowball" wrong - often laughably.

whoa.headline: Are major ocean currents moving to turn Earth into a snowball?
whoa.summary: One of Earth's most vital ocean currents is rapidly weakening. The cause: global warming. A collapse of this current could send devastating ripples through the planet's climate.

whoa.headline: NASA spacecraft discovers a huge new crater on the moon
whoa.summary: Scientists have discovered a crater on the moon that's bigger than the Roman Colosseum and is the result of a powerful impact two years ago that initially went undetected.

whoa.headline: Snow, monsoons and oceans shift Earth's center of mass each year, satellite tracking shows
whoa.summary: Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet's center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth's center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements.

whoa.headline: Indonesia's Anak Krakatau
whoa.summary: Anak Krakatau erupts ash and volcanic gases in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 on Sept. 5, 2026.

whoa.headline: Some Fish in the Great Lakes Might Be More Than 400 Years Old, a Study Suggests, Outliving Around 15 Generations of Humans
whoa.summary: Lake sturgeon may be among the longest-living vertebrates, second only to Greenland sharks, according to recent research. However, scientists note that follow-up work is necessary to clarify the species' lifespan

whoa.headline: Diplodocus dinosaur discovered in Europe for the first time
whoa.summary: Until now, fossils of the huge long-necked plant-eating dino had only ever been uncovered in North America. Find out more here.

whoa.headline: UK butterfly numbers are up but campaigners say it's not all good news
whoa.summary: Warm weather have seen butterfly numbers grow in the UK this year, but charity Butterfly Conservation are worried about a population crash.

whoa.headline: Why are shops moving Pokémon cards and popular toys behind the till?
whoa.summary: Dozens of shops have moved popular products away from open shelves, as new figures reveal more than half a million recorded shoplifting offences.

whoa.headline: Watch an orca smash into a sunfish hard enough to make it explode
whoa.summary: Orcas have been known to slap around stingrays, punt seals into the air and otherwise play with their food. But orcas, or killer whales, don't just toy with live prey . Some also seem to enjoy destroying the corpses of their kills like piñatas.

whoa.headline: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
whoa.summary: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars's south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it's a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet.

whoa.headline: US acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
whoa.summary: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes.

whoa.headline: Special Pokémon cards being released for 30th birthday
whoa.summary: Collectors and fans will be hunting down the special release, which marks 30 years since the card game first started.

whoa.headline: A world 20 light-years away reveals surprisingly organized, Jupiter-like weather
whoa.summary: Scientists from Trinity College Dublin have developed a way to unravel changing weather patterns on distant worlds. Using this approach, they discovered that the weather on a well-studied brown dwarf, SIMP 0136, previously linked to northern lights-like phenomena, is largely shaped by just two dominant processes: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.

whoa.headline: Strictly is back: Are you ready for the revamp?
whoa.summary: There'll be new hosts, as well as change-ups among the professional dancers, and of course a new group of celebrities joining too! But are you ready for the brand new look? Here's all we know so far.

whoa.headline: Your Planet: Environmental news from around the world
whoa.summary: This week on Your Planet, a rare snail makes a comeback in the UK, why scientists are keeping a close eye on seahorses and seagrass, and the unusual turtles making a special arrival in Mexico.

whoa.headline: Artemis III Crew Visits NASA Kennedy's Vehicle Assembly Building
whoa.summary: NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik (left) and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano view progress on the solid rocket booster integration in High Bay 3 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026.

whoa.headline: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
whoa.summary: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.

whoa.headline: Finally! How to get a truly random number - and prove it
whoa.summary: Every time someone attempts to create an unbreakable password or send a private message, they must trust a number. That number is supposed to be one that a computer has generated completely at random. Unfortunately, no computer has been able to actually guarantee that this number is truly random.

whoa.headline: NASA Kicks Off Inspiration Tour with Steelers vs. Falcons Game
whoa.summary: Fans pose for a photo with an astronaut in the NASA Experience Zone at an NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Atlanta Falcons at Acrisure Stadium, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

whoa.headline: Monkeys might share our instincts for math
whoa.summary: There are some skills that people think set us apart from other animals. These usually include language, tool use or the ability to do some types of math. But at least some cows can use tools and cockatoos can make their own .

whoa.headline: Scientists Say: Mammal
whoa.summary: Mammal (noun, "MAM-mal") Mammals are a diverse group of animals. They include about 6,600 known, living species . Many of them, including humans, cats and dogs, live on land.

whoa.headline: No cities on the moon - there isn't enough water, scientists say
whoa.summary: The discovery of water in dark craters at the moon's poles has sparked a "moon rush" to establish bases there, followed by villages, cities and heavy industry. How sustainable is this rush?

whoa.headline: JWST ruled out finding tiny moons around an exoplanet - that's great news
whoa.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has opened many wonders of the cosmos to scientists since it began science operations a few years ago. But one thing it hasn't done is find an "exomoon." These still-theoretical moons orbit exoplanets in other star systems, and JWST was supposed to find a plethora of them.

whoa.headline: Could dino poo unlock answers to ancient bird mystery?
whoa.summary: Scientists believe that a very old poo containing bird feathers could help shed light on the reason why many bird species died out millions of years ago.

whoa.headline: Japan's Hayabusa2 achieves first-ever laser ranging experiment with an asteroid
whoa.summary: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Hayabusa2 spacecraft reached another milestone this summer, a first for space agencies. On Sunday, July 5, the probe conducted the first successful laser-ranging experiment during a flyby of asteroid Torifune, the first exploration target of Hayabusa2's Extended Mission. This latest milestone will advance the capabilities of JAXA and other space agencies as they pursue future missions involving near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) and other deep-space objects.

wins.headline: The ozone hole is shrinking
wins.summary: Countries banned the chemicals that were eating the sky's sunscreen. Scientists now measure the hole getting smaller. A giant problem, slowly reversing.
wins.try: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.
wins.tryLine: The move was a treaty plus better fridges. Teamwork at planet scale.

wins.headline: Humpback whales came back from the brink
wins.summary: Hunting nearly wiped them out. Bans and watchers gave them decades of quiet. Many populations have rebounded enough that boats now have to share the water.
wins.try: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.
wins.tryLine: If you ever whale-watch, look for the tail fluke. Each one is unique.

wins.headline: Kids' blood lead levels crashed
wins.summary: Lead in petrol and paint used to quietly hurt brains. Laws pulled it out. Average levels in many countries fell hard. Policy can be a superpower.
wins.try: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.
wins.tryLine: Old houses can still have lead paint. That's a grown-up check, not a kid job.

wins.headline: Humans wiped one killer disease off Earth
wins.summary: Smallpox used to scar and kill millions. Vaccines plus a worldwide hunt ended it in 1980. It is the only human disease we have fully erased.
wins.try: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.
wins.tryLine: That is what 'the plan worked' looks like at planet size.

wins.headline: Some rivers got otters back
wins.summary: Cleaner water and protection let otters return to rivers that were empty. If you see one, that's a report card for the whole valley.
wins.try: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.
wins.tryLine: A local wildlife page will tell you if otters live near you.

wins.headline: Solar got cheap enough to flood the grid
wins.summary: Panels used to be a rich-country toy. Prices crashed. Now whole countries add solar faster than coal. The physics did not change. The cost did.
wins.try: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.
wins.tryLine: Spot three roofs with panels on your next walk.

wins.headline: Kids ran a little free library street
wins.summary: A box on a lawn. Take a book, leave a book. Some streets now have three. No app, no fee, just neighbours trusting kids with stories.
wins.try: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.
wins.tryLine: If you pass one, swap one book. That's the whole game.

wins.headline: Some coral is being grown in nurseries
wins.summary: Divers farm hardy coral and glue it back onto damaged reef. Not a full fix. It is a start, and fish move back in.
wins.try: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.
wins.tryLine: Reef-safe sunscreen exists. That's a tiny assist.

wins.headline: Cities that built bike lanes got more bikes
wins.summary: Paint and kerbs changed who dared to ride. Kids included. Safer paths, more riders, fewer cars on short trips. Design beats nagging.
wins.try: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.
wins.tryLine: Count bike lanes on your school route. Zero is a clue.

wins.headline: Bag charges slashed plastic at the till
wins.summary: A few pence changed habits faster than posters. Many countries saw single-use bags crash. Small price, huge pile of plastic not made.
wins.try: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.
wins.tryLine: Keep one tote by the door. Future-you will grab it.

wins.headline: A teen built a cheaper hearing test
wins.summary: Julian Wilson and others have built simple phone-based hearing checks so more kids get spotted early. Not a hospital. A screen and a plan.
wins.try: If someone talks loud at you a lot, a hearing check is kindness, not teasing.

wins.headline: Beavers got invited back on purpose
wins.summary: They build wetlands that soak floods and help fish. Some rivers that were ditches now hold water again. A rodent as infrastructure.
wins.try: Look up a beaver dam photo. That's a living dam.
wins.tryLine: Look up a beaver dam photo. That's a living dam.

wins.headline: Dark-sky towns switched the lights down
wins.summary: Warmer, downward lamps cut glare. Stars came back. Turtles and owls got a quieter night. You can still see the pavement.
wins.try: On a clear night, count stars in one window of sky.
wins.tryLine: On a clear night, count stars in one window of sky.

wins.headline: Kids redesigned their own playground
wins.summary: Some schools asked pupils to map the boring bits, then rebuild. More climbing, more shade, fewer 'don't'. Behaviour got better because the place got better.
wins.try: Sketch one change that would make your break better. That's a brief.

wins.headline: A seed in a jar is a tiny win farm
wins.summary: Wet kitchen paper, a bean, a window. In days you get a root. Proof you can grow something on purpose.
wins.try: Start one bean tonight. Name it something silly.
wins.tryLine: Start one bean tonight. Name it something silly.

wins.headline: A good apology is a win, not a loss
wins.summary: Name the thing, skip the excuse, ask how to fix it. People remember the repair more than the mess. That's how teams stay teams.

harvest.headline: Five Ways the World of the Dinosaurs Looked Different From Ours, Beyond the Presence of the 'Terrible Lizards'
harvest.summary: Earth has changed dramatically since the Age of Dinosaurs, from its climate to geography and animal life

harvest.headline: The human brain may owe a lot of its size to our love of sweets
harvest.summary: Our sweets cravings may have set the stage for the human brain to become big and powerful. That's the finding of a new study. The brains of our upright-walking ancestors, some 4 million years ago, weighed only around 300 grams (11 ounces).

harvest.headline: A galaxy spinning out of sync
harvest.summary: Image: Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It's one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.

harvest.headline: A modern 'snowball' Earth? What the movies get wrong
harvest.summary: Earth has frozen over in the past - at least five times. Science fiction is full of takes about how it might happen again and the implications of a modern ice age. The problem: At a minimum, sci-fi gets the timetable for Earth turning into a "snowball" wrong - often laughably.

harvest.headline: Are major ocean currents moving to turn Earth into a snowball?
harvest.summary: One of Earth's most vital ocean currents is rapidly weakening. The cause: global warming. A collapse of this current could send devastating ripples through the planet's climate.

harvest.headline: Some Fish in the Great Lakes Might Be More Than 400 Years Old, a Study Suggests, Outliving Around 15 Generations of Humans
harvest.summary: Lake sturgeon may be among the longest-living vertebrates, second only to Greenland sharks, according to recent research. However, scientists note that follow-up work is necessary to clarify the species' lifespan

harvest.headline: Purple swirls on the Red Planet
harvest.summary: This image shows a prominent ice cliff near Mars's south pole. With striking swirls of purple, pink and red, it's a far cry from the colour palette we usually associate with the Red Planet.

harvest.headline: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
harvest.summary: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.

harvest.headline: Peptides Are All the Rage, Promising Miracle Cures and Makeovers Delivered by Injection. How Did We Get Here?
harvest.summary: Experts say the peptide craze is part of a broader phenomenon, as patients look beyond the regulated health system to address problems that doctors have struggled to treat

harvest.headline: Perseverance Selfie with Ingenuity
harvest.summary: On the Mars rover's mission Sol 46 or Earth date April 6, 2021, Perseverance held out a robotic arm to take its first selfie on Mars. The WATSON camera at the end of the arm was designed to take close-ups of Martian rocks and surface details though, and not a quick snap shot of friends and smiling faces. harvest.headline: Shells and Arcs around Star CW Leonis
harvest.summary: What's happening around this star? No one is sure. CW Leonis is the closest carbon star, a star that appears orange because of atmospheric carbon dispersed from interior nuclear fusion. But CW Leonis also appears engulfed in a gaseous carbon-rich nebula. What causes the nebula's complexity is unknown, but its geometry of shells and arcs are surely intriguing. harvest.headline: Saturn's Iapetus: Moon with a Strange Surface
harvest.summary: What would make a moon look like a walnut? A strange ridge that circles Saturn's moon Iapetus's equator, visible near the bottom of the featured image, makes it appear similar to a popular edible nut. The origin of the ridge remains unknown, though, with hypotheses including ice that welled up from below, a ring that crashed down from above, and structure left over from its formation perhaps 100 million years ago. harvest.headline: RoboCup 2026: Why are robots playing football in Germany?
harvest.summary: RoboCup 2026 took place in Germany this year. BBC reporter Andrew Rogers was there and asked a robotics expert all about it.

harvest.headline: Happy News: Stories to make you smile
harvest.summary: De-Graft has this week's Happy News. We are visiting an autumnal festival in Vietnam, a community garden in Australia and meeting some showbiz pumpkins in Germany.

harvest.headline: Venus ate its moon: How Earth's 'twin' could have swallowed a rocky satellite
harvest.summary: Scientists have long speculated why Venus, with a size, mass and structure similar to Earth's, doesn't have a moon. New UC Riverside research shows that our hungry twin likely swallowed it.

harvest.headline: To understand the solar cycle, notice how the sun sleeps
harvest.summary: The sun is such a constant in our lives that it can be difficult to imagine our star ever changing. But the sun can be quite variable. There are times when its magnetic field is turbulent and generates many sunspots and other times when it is quiet and dormant.

harvest.headline: Strictly is back - were you watching?
harvest.summary: Fifteen celebrities have joined for the 24th series, but this year there have been some changes with celebs partnered with their professionals dancers in a new way and there have also been changes to the presenting line-up. Let us know what you thought of this year's launch show.

harvest.headline: COSI Telescope Comes Together
harvest.summary: UC Berkeley engineers and managers watch as the COSI (Compton Spectrometer and Imager) detector assembly is slowly raised from a table in this July 8, 2026, image.

harvest.headline: NASA Unveils Enterprise, the First Space Shuttle
harvest.summary: The rollout ceremony for NASA's first space shuttle, OV-101, coincided with Constitution Day of the nation's bicentennial on Sept.17, 1976. Although the orbiter was originally planned to be named Constitution, Star Trek fans successfully convinced President Gerald Ford to name it Enterprise after the series' fictional starship.

harvest.headline: Indonesia's Anak Krakatau
harvest.summary: Anak Krakatau erupts ash and volcanic gases in this image acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 on Sept. 5, 2026.
